assessments.technical_explanation: The CI workflow calls a reusable build workflow located in the same repository and passes all repository secrets via blanket inheritance. The workflow only triggers on schedule, pushes to the default branch, and manual dispatch, so untrusted pull-request code never reaches it. The called workflow is maintained by the same maintainers in the same repository, so an attacker who could alter it to abuse inherited secrets would already need write access to the repository. The weakness is that every secret is forwarded rather than only the specific ones the build needs, which widens the blast radius of any future compromise of the called workflow and makes secret usage less auditable.

assessments.developer_action: Replace blanket secrets inheritance with explicit passthrough of only the secrets each build workflow requires, so that future changes to the called workflows cannot silently gain access to unrelated secrets.

assessments.technical_explanation: The release body parameter uses a pseudo-ternary whose intended empty-string result is falsy, so the fallback text is always selected, including on re-runs where the intent was to leave the body unset so existing draft notes are preserved. This is a logic defect in workflow expression handling, not a security control: the affected value is release-note text visible to the public, no secrets or untrusted input are involved, and the release remains a draft until a guarded publish step. The concrete effect is that draft notes typed into a re-run pre-release can be overwritten with the placeholder text.
assessments.layman_explanation: A conditional expression used to decide the release description is written in a way that always picks the fallback text, so the intended keep-existing-notes behavior on re-runs does not happen. assessments.developer_action: Replace the empty-string pseudo-ternary with an explicit conditional, for example an if/else at job level or a step that sets the body only when the release is not already a draft, so an empty body is actually preserved.

assessments.technical_explanation: The matched 64-hex-character value is a fallback search token for the JannyAI character-discovery provider. The code's primary path fetches the token live by scraping JannyAI's own public, client-side JavaScript config, which by design ships this token to every browser visitor of that site. The hardcoded value is a cached copy of that same public token, used only as a Bearer header against the third-party search endpoint when the live scrape fails. It is not a user credential, not a project secret, and is not sent anywhere except the third-party service it belongs to. This matches the stated purpose of a character-discovery provider. The weakness is maintainability and fragility: the token is not a user secret but will silently break search if the third party rotates it, and its presence invites scanner noise. There is no demonstrated exposure of user data, credentials, or an attacker-controlled path to concrete harm.
assessments.layman_explanation: The flagged string is a search-access token for a public character-browsing website. That site publishes the same token to every visitor of its own pages, and this app uses it only to search that site's catalog. It is not the user's password or API key, and it does not go anywhere unexpected. At worst, if the site changes the token, the app's search feature stops working until updated.
assessments.developer_action: Document in code that this token is a public client-side value belonging to the third-party site, not a secret, and consider a gitleaks allowlist entry to suppress future flags. Optionally handle token rotation gracefully rather than relying on a hardcoded fallback.

assessments.technical_explanation: The matched value is a 64-hex-character bearer token hardcoded as a fallback in a production discovery-provider module. The data flow shows the provider first tries to scrape the same token live from the third-party character-site's public client-side JavaScript bundle (which is served to every visitor of that site), and only falls back to the embedded copy. This is a search-index access token belonging to the external site, not a credential belonging to the project, its users, or any user-configured provider key; it is sent only to that site's own search endpoint, which matches the stated discovery feature. No project or user secret is exposed and no exfiltration path exists. The weakness is maintainability and hygiene: a hardcoded third-party token can silently expire, and scraping a token out of another site's page markup is fragile. It does not demonstrate a concrete attacker-controlled path to meaningful harm for users.
assessments.layman_explanation: The code contains a long access code for another website's public search feature. That website already hands the same code to every visitor's browser, so it is not a private password of the app, its developers, or its users. It is only used to search that site, which is what the feature is for. The main downside is that the built-in copy can go stale and the search could stop working.
assessments.developer_action: Consider documenting that this is a third-party site's publicly distributed search token rather than a project secret, and marking the fallback for the secrets scanner so future audits are not misled. Prefer relying on the live token fetch where possible.

assessments.technical_explanation: The desktop build job in the pre-release workflow inherits the full repository secret set for a same-repository reusable workflow. The workflow only starts on maintainer-pushed version tags or manual dispatch, and the reusable workflow is in the same maintainer-controlled repository, so no attacker-controlled execution path receives the secrets. The over-broad forwarding is a least-privilege gap that would enlarge the damage if the called workflow were ever compromised or maliciously edited, which itself requires repository write access.
assessments.layman_explanation: The desktop test-build job also receives every stored secret instead of only the ones it needs. It only runs when maintainers trigger it and the receiving script is in the same repository, so this is a least-privilege cleanup item, not an exploitable flaw.
assessments.developer_action: Pass explicit named secrets required for desktop packaging instead of blanket inheritance.

assessments.technical_explanation: The release body value is built with a pseudo-ternary whose empty-string branch is falsy, so the fallback placeholder text is always chosen, defeating the documented intent of leaving the body unset on re-runs so that manually typed draft notes are preserved. This is a workflow-logic defect affecting only public release-note text; no secrets, untrusted input, or security boundary are involved, and the release stays a draft until manually published. The concrete harm is limited to possible overwriting of typed release notes with a generic placeholder.
assessments.layman_explanation: A conditional expression meant to preserve existing release notes on a re-run is written so that the fallback text always wins. The result is that typed notes could be replaced by a generic line. That is a small functional bug in the release process, not a security problem.
assessments.developer_action: Rework the body selection so the empty case is genuinely unset, for example by computing the body in a separate conditional step that emits no body value when the release is already a draft.

observations.title: Hardcoded fallback token duplicates a value the third-party site already publishes publicly
observations.technical_explanation: The live token-acquisition routine fetches and parses the token from the provider's public client config script, showing the token is intended to be public. The constant is only used as a fallback Bearer credential for the same third-party search endpoint, with no other destination. Download URLs from the API are additionally constrained to a fixed allowlist of hosts and plain HTTPS with no port, limiting response-controlled fetch destinations.
observations.layman_explanation: The token is one the target website itself hands out to every visitor, kept here as a backup. It is only ever used to talk to that same website, and the code even restricts downloads to that site's approved addresses.
observations.developer_action: Add a comment or scanner suppression noting the token is public third-party data, and prefer failing over to a fresh fetch or clearer error when the fallback expires.
